items.prompt: What is an objection, in the sense this unit uses the term?
choices: A reason a prospect gives for not moving forward right now
A formal rejection that ends the deal permanently, with no realistic path back to a yes
A technical bug report a prospect files about something broken in a trial or demo environment
A request for a refund submitted by a customer sometime after the purchase was completed
items.explanation: An objection is a stated reason for pausing, not a final no. Treating it as a request for more information, rather than a wall, is what makes the acknowledge → isolate → reframe structure work at all.
items.reference:
🗣️ objection = a stated reason to pause, not 🚫 a final no

Why: An objection is a request for more information, even when it's phrased like a flat refusal — treating it that way is what let Rep B's real gap surface in L1's opening scenario.

items.prompt: Rep A and Rep B in L1's opening scenario got the identical objection line from the same prospect. What separated Rep B's response from treating it as a rejection?
choices: Rep B treated the line as a request to unpack, not a wall to argue through
Rep B offered a discount immediately, before asking any follow-up question at all
Rep B ignored the objection entirely and kept walking through the feature list
Rep B ended the call politely and said they'd follow up again sometime next week
items.explanation: Rep B agreed the point was fair, then asked what still cost the prospect time — treating the line as an opening to ask more, not a closed door. That's the difference between hearing an objection as information versus as a rejection.
items.reference:
🗣️ objection = a stated reason to pause, not 🚫 a final no

Why: An objection is a request for more information, even when it's phrased like a flat refusal — treating it that way is what let Rep B's real gap surface in L1's opening scenario.

items.prompt: What is status quo bias, as it applies to "we already have something that works"?
choices: Preferring the current option because its flaws are already known and survivable, even if it isn't the best option
Always choosing whichever option happens to cost the least amount of money upfront
A bias that, per this unit, only ever affects irrational or inexperienced buyers
A negotiating tactic that reps themselves deliberately deploy against prospects
items.explanation: Status quo bias is preferring the familiar option because its problems are known and survivable, while a new option's problems are unknown — not a sign the prospect is being irrational, and not something a rep does to a prospect.
items.reference:
🏠 known flaws feel safer than 🆕 unknown ones

Why: Status quo bias explains why "we already have something that works" is often reflexive — the current system's flaws feel survivable precisely because they're already known.

items.prompt: Why does a prospect often raise "we already have something that works" almost reflexively, even when the current system has real, costly gaps?
choices: Status quo bias — the familiar option's flaws are already known, which feels safer than an unknown new option's flaws
Because most prospects raising this line are really just trying to negotiate a lower price
Because the current system in place is, in every case, objectively the better option
Because most reps tend to pitch too early in the conversation, before trust is built
items.explanation: The line is often a reflex tied to status quo bias, not a considered judgment that the current system is actually better — which is exactly why isolating (asking what still costs time) can surface a real gap the prospect hadn't led with.
items.reference:
🏠 known flaws feel safer than 🆕 unknown ones

Why: Status quo bias explains why "we already have something that works" is often reflexive — the current system's flaws feel survivable precisely because they're already known.

items.prompt: In L1's opening scenario, why did arguing feature-by-feature against the incumbent (Rep A) make the prospect more defensive rather than less?
choices: Arguing treated the objection as a wall to argue through, putting the prospect in a position of defending a decision they'd already made
Because Rep A's product genuinely had fewer features than the incumbent being replaced
Because Rep A spent too long talking before letting the prospect respond on the call
Because Rep A quoted a price that came in higher than the prospect had expected
items.explanation: Arguing signals "I heard a wall, not a person," which makes a prospect defend a decision they've already made harder — the opposite of opening the conversation up.
items.reference:
⚔️ argue back → prospect gets defensive
🤝 acknowledge first → prospect opens up

Why: Arguing immediately signals "I heard a wall, not a person" and makes a prospect defend a decision already made; acknowledging first keeps the conversation open long enough for the real concern to surface.

items.prompt: What did Rep B do in the first ten seconds after hearing the objection that Rep A did not?
choices: Acknowledged the point was fair before asking a follow-up question, instead of contesting it right away
Offered an immediate discount to try to keep the prospect engaged on the call itself
Asked the prospect to walk through their entire current workflow in detail first
Ended the call right away and said they'd follow up again later by email
items.explanation: Rep B validated the objection as reasonable before asking anything else, which is the acknowledge step — buying trust before probing further, rather than contesting the point immediately.
items.reference:
⚔️ argue back → prospect gets defensive
🤝 acknowledge first → prospect opens up

Why: Arguing immediately signals "I heard a wall, not a person" and makes a prospect defend a decision already made; acknowledging first keeps the conversation open long enough for the real concern to surface.

items.prompt: What's the risk of treating an objection as a wall to argue through, rather than a request for more information?
choices: The prospect defends their existing position harder instead of examining it, which tends to close off the conversation rather than open it
The call simply takes noticeably longer to finish than it otherwise would have
The rep eventually runs out of features left to compare against the incumbent
The prospect ends up asking for a bigger discount than they otherwise would have
items.explanation: Arguing pushes a prospect to defend a decision they've already made, which closes the conversation down rather than opening it — the opposite effect of an acknowledging, question-first response.
items.reference:
⚔️ argue back → prospect gets defensive
🤝 acknowledge first → prospect opens up

Why: Arguing immediately signals "I heard a wall, not a person" and makes a prospect defend a decision already made; acknowledging first keeps the conversation open long enough for the real concern to surface.

items.prompt: According to this unit, why is "it's too expensive" often not really a pure budget fact?
choices: The prospect frequently hasn't seen enough value yet to justify the number, rather than the number being literally unaffordable
Because reps at most companies tend to price their product too high from the start
Because prospects, per this unit, never actually have a real, fixed budget at all
Because price objections are, per this unit, always just a bluff to test the rep
items.explanation: A price objection is often standing in for an unproven value case, not a literal budget ceiling — which is exactly why isolating (asking which one it is) matters before responding.
items.reference:
💰 real budget ceiling
🤔 value case not yet proven

Why: Both sound like "too expensive." An instant discount treats it as always a budget fact — isolating first tells you which one you're actually facing.

items.prompt: If a rep immediately offers a discount the moment a prospect says "it's too expensive," what important distinction gets skipped?
choices: Whether the number itself is genuinely outside the prospect's actual, fixed budget range
Whether the prospect would rather be billed monthly or annually going forward
Whether the prospect has already spoken with one of the rep's competitors
Whether the deal in question needs a manager's sign-off before it can close
items.explanation: Jumping straight to a discount skips finding out whether the real issue is budget or an unproven value case — and a discount doesn't fix the second one at all.
items.reference:
💰 real budget ceiling
🤔 value case not yet proven

Why: Both sound like "too expensive." An instant discount treats it as always a budget fact — isolating first tells you which one you're actually facing.

items.prompt: How does this unit relate to the related "buyer psychology" unit?
choices: Buyer psychology diagnoses the real hesitation beneath a stated objection; objection handling is what to say and do live once the objection is spoken aloud
They are two different names for exactly the same skill
Buyer psychology is, per this unit, only useful before an objection is raised, with no relevance once one actually lands
Objection handling, per this unit, replaces the need for buyer psychology entirely once a rep is experienced enough
items.explanation: The two units are sequential: buyer psychology is about decoding why a hesitation exists underneath what's said; objection handling picks up from there with what to actually say and do in the live conversation.
items.reference:
🔍 buyer psychology = diagnose the "why" underneath
🗣️ objection handling = what to say/do live

Why: The two units are sequential, not overlapping — one explains the hesitation underneath, the other is the real-time response once it's spoken aloud.

items.prompt: Why does this unit assume the diagnostic work of "buyer psychology" is happening already or in parallel, rather than covering it itself?
choices: Because objection handling is about the live conversation response, not diagnosing the underlying hesitation, which is a distinct related skill
Because buyer psychology is, per this unit, considered a less important skill than objection handling overall
Because the two units, per this unit's framing, cover two completely unrelated sales topics
Because diagnosing hesitation, per this unit, only actually matters after a deal has already closed
items.explanation: This unit's scope is deliberately the live response once an objection is on the table — the diagnostic work of reading a prospect's underlying hesitation is buyer psychology's territory, not repeated here.
items.reference:
🔍 buyer psychology = diagnose the "why" underneath
🗣️ objection handling = what to say/do live

Why: The two units are sequential, not overlapping — one explains the hesitation underneath, the other is the real-time response once it's spoken aloud.

items.prompt: What are the two objections this unit names as the most common a rep hears?
choices: "We already have something that works" (status quo) and "it's too expensive" (price)
'We need to think about it a little more' and 'can you send over some extra documentation'
'I don't have the authority to decide this' and 'call me back again next quarter'
'Your competitor is cheaper than you are' and 'we've had a bad experience before'
items.explanation: The two objections named directly in this unit's title, and used as the running examples throughout, are the status quo objection and the price objection.
items.reference:
🗣️ "we already have something that works" (status quo)
💵 "it's too expensive" (price)

Why: These two show up across almost every deal in some form, which is why acknowledge → isolate → reframe is built to generalize to both, and to most other objections too.

items.prompt: This unit's title names two specific objections. Which pairing matches it?
choices: A status quo objection and a price objection
A timing objection paired with a decision-making authority objection
A trust-in-the-vendor objection paired with a direct competitor objection
A feature-gap objection paired with a support-quality complaint objection
items.explanation: The title itself is built from the status quo objection ("we already have something that works") and the price objection ("it's too expensive") — the two running examples across L1–L3.
items.reference:
🗣️ "we already have something that works" (status quo)
💵 "it's too expensive" (price)

Why: These two show up across almost every deal in some form, which is why acknowledge → isolate → reframe is built to generalize to both, and to most other objections too.

items.prompt: What is the correct order of the acknowledge → isolate → reframe structure, and why does the order matter?
choices: Acknowledge first to keep the prospect from getting defensive, isolate second to find the real blocker, reframe last with substance once you know what you're responding to
Reframe first with the strongest available counterpoint, then acknowledge, then isolate afterward
Isolate first to find the blocker, then reframe immediately, acknowledging only if the reframe fails
The order doesn't actually matter, per this unit, as long as all three steps happen somewhere in the call
items.explanation: Each step depends on the one before it: acknowledging keeps the prospect from getting defensive and willing to keep talking, isolating finds out what's actually blocking a decision, and reframe only makes sense once you know what you're responding to.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Acknowledge→2️⃣ Isolate→3️⃣ Reframe

Why: Each step depends on the one before it — acknowledging keeps the door open, isolating tells you what's actually on the other side of it, and reframe only works once you know that.

items.prompt: A rep skips straight to reframe — a value-based response — right after an objection lands, without acknowledging or isolating first. What's the practical risk?
choices: The reframe might target the wrong concern, since isolate hadn't confirmed what's actually blocking the decision yet
The call will simply end up taking longer than it strictly needed to, per this unit
The prospect will assume, per this unit, that the rep hasn't been properly trained
There is no real risk here, since reframe is, per this unit, the step that actually resolves it
items.explanation: Reframing before isolating risks answering a concern the prospect doesn't actually have — the isolate step is what confirms the target before spending the reframe on it.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Acknowledge→2️⃣ Isolate→3️⃣ Reframe

Why: Each step depends on the one before it — acknowledging keeps the door open, isolating tells you what's actually on the other side of it, and reframe only works once you know that.

items.prompt: Why must isolate happen before reframe, rather than after?
choices: Reframe only makes sense once you know what you're actually responding to — reframing before isolating risks answering a concern the prospect doesn't have
Because isolate, per this unit, simply takes less time to execute than reframe does
Because prospects expect questions before substantive answers, regardless of the content
There's no real dependency between the two steps — the order is purely a stylistic preference
items.explanation: Isolate is what tells a rep which concern to actually reframe against — doing reframe first risks solving a problem the prospect never had, while the real one goes unaddressed.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Acknowledge→2️⃣ Isolate→3️⃣ Reframe

Why: Each step depends on the one before it — acknowledging keeps the door open, isolating tells you what's actually on the other side of it, and reframe only works once you know that.

items.prompt: What specific failure does the "isolate" step catch that both arguing-immediately and caving-immediately skip?
choices: Whether the stated objection is the only thing blocking a yes, or a stand-in for something the prospect hasn't said yet
Whether the prospect actually has enough authority within their company to sign a contract
Whether the competitor's product is, in objective terms, actually cheaper than this one
Whether the call has run long enough already to justify scheduling a follow-up
items.explanation: Isolate directly checks whether the stated objection is the real, complete blocker — both bad responses (arguing, caving) skip straight past that question entirely.
items.reference:
🔍 isolate = "is this THE blocker, or one of several?"

Why: Both bad responses (arguing, caving) skip straight past this question, either fighting or paying for a concern that was never confirmed as the real one.

items.prompt: A prospect says "it's too expensive" and the rep immediately offers 10% off, skipping isolate entirely. What real risk does that create?
choices: The rep might give away margin without confirming whether price was even the real blocker, and the discount might not actually fix anything
The prospect will, per this unit, always accept the discount immediately, ending the call too fast
The reframe step becomes, per this unit, impossible to perform later in the same conversation
The rep loses the ability to acknowledge the objection again later on in the call
items.explanation: Skipping isolate means the discount is a guess at the real problem — if the prospect actually hadn't seen enough value yet, the same prospect can come back next month just as unconvinced, at a lower price.
items.reference:
🔍 isolate = "is this THE blocker, or one of several?"

Why: Both bad responses (arguing, caving) skip straight past this question, either fighting or paying for a concern that was never confirmed as the real one.

items.prompt: Per L2's comparison table, what does the strong response to "it's too expensive" actually say?
choices: "Is the number itself outside budget, or is it that we haven't shown enough value yet to justify it?"
'I can knock 10% off the price right now if that would help move things along faster'
'Let me walk you through every single feature again in a bit more detail'
'I'll need to check with my manager on that and get back to you later'
items.explanation: The strong response is an isolating question, not an immediate concession — it asks before it gives anything away, which is what determines whether the real fix is a lower price or a better reframe of value.
items.reference:
❌ weak — "10% off right now"
✅ strong — "is it budget, or unproven value?"

Why: The strong version asks before it gives anything away; the weak version gives something away before it knows what's actually wrong.

items.prompt: What's wrong with the weak response "I can knock 10% off if that helps" to a price objection?
choices: It skips both acknowledge and isolate, treating a possibly-unconvinced value case as if it were a fixed, real budget fact
10% is, per this unit's framing, generally just too small a discount to matter to most prospects
It's technically correct as a response, just phrased a bit less politely than it needs to be
It reveals the rep's true list price to the prospect earlier than it should in the conversation
items.explanation: The weak response assumes the objection is purely about the number, without ever checking — which means it might give away margin for a problem that discounting doesn't actually solve.
items.reference:
❌ weak — "10% off right now"
✅ strong — "is it budget, or unproven value?"

Why: The strong version asks before it gives anything away; the weak version gives something away before it knows what's actually wrong.

items.prompt: Per L2's comparison table, what does the strong response to "we already have something that works" actually say?
choices: "Makes sense, switching costs are real — is there anything about the current setup that still costs you time, even if it's mostly working?"
'Here's why we come out ahead of the incumbent on every single feature that matters'
'What would it actually take to get you to switch over to us today?'
'Plenty of our competitors' own customers end up switching over to us eventually'
items.explanation: The strong response acknowledges the switching cost is real, then asks an open isolating question — rather than arguing the current system's flaws point by point.
items.reference:
❌ weak — "we're better on every feature"
✅ strong — "is there anything that still costs you time?"

Why: Arguing invites defense; asking invites disclosure of a real, specific gap.

items.prompt: What's wrong with the weak response "Here's why we're better on every feature" to the incumbent objection?
choices: It argues against the prospect's existing choice instead of acknowledging it, making them defend the decision rather than examine it
It's simply too short a response to be persuasive in the middle of a live call
It reveals competitive information about the rep's own product that the prospect shouldn't have
It skips describing the product's actual features in any real amount of detail
items.explanation: Feature-by-feature argument puts the prospect in a position of defending a decision they've already made, closing the conversation down rather than opening it up to a real gap.
items.reference:
❌ weak — "we're better on every feature"
✅ strong — "is there anything that still costs you time?"

Why: Arguing invites defense; asking invites disclosure of a real, specific gap.

items.prompt: What defines a real concession trade, as opposed to a plain discount?
choices: Something is given up (like a lower price) only in exchange for something received back — a longer term, a reference, faster payment
The rep, per this unit's definition, always gives up more value than the prospect receives back
Concessions must, per this unit, always be offered before the prospect has asked for one
A trade, per this unit, requires involving a manager or formal approval process every time
items.explanation: A concession trade is defined by the exchange — give something, get something back — which keeps it a negotiation instead of a one-way giveaway.
items.reference:
⚖️ give X (discount) ↔ get Y (longer term / reference / faster payment)

Why: A trade keeps the exchange a negotiation; a one-way discount trains the other side that your price was never real.

items.prompt: Why does a one-way discount risk more than just the lost margin?
choices: It trains the prospect that the original price was never real, inviting them to ask for more next time, with nothing received in return
It usually ends up violating a company's standard sales compliance rules and policies
It makes the reframe step, per this unit, impossible to use later on in the conversation
It has, per this unit, no additional risk beyond the lost margin on that single deal
items.explanation: A one-way discount signals the price was negotiable from the start with nothing asked in return, setting a precedent that invites further requests — unlike a trade, which exchanges value both ways.
items.reference:
⚖️ give X (discount) ↔ get Y (longer term / reference / faster payment)

Why: A trade keeps the exchange a negotiation; a one-way discount trains the other side that your price was never real.

items.prompt: What does "anchoring" mean in a price negotiation, per L2?
choices: The first number stated in a negotiation pulls the rest of the conversation toward it
A rep refusing to move off their originally quoted price under any circumstances at all
A prospect's budget being completely fixed and impossible to change during a negotiation
A discount that gets offered automatically at the very end of every single sales call
items.explanation: Anchoring is the effect where the first number spoken — by either side — pulls the rest of the negotiation toward it, which is why who says a number first, and how it's followed up, matters.
items.reference:
🎯 the first number said pulls the rest of the conversation toward it

Why: A counter-offer with reasoning behind it resets the anchor; just negotiating down from someone else's number lets their number keep steering.

items.prompt: A prospect opens with "can you do 20% off?" before the rep has stated any number. What is this an example of, and what's the recommended response?
choices: The prospect anchoring first — the right response is a reasoned counter-offer, not just a smaller discount, to reset the anchor
A price objection that should, per this unit, be met with immediate agreement to the number
A sign, per this unit, that the deal is simply not worth pursuing any further
A request that should, per this unit, always be declined outright with no counter at all
items.explanation: The prospect naming a number first is itself an anchor — the recommended response is a counter-offer backed by reasoning, which resets the anchor around value rather than just haggling down from their number.
items.reference:
🎯 the first number said pulls the rest of the conversation toward it

Why: A counter-offer with reasoning behind it resets the anchor; just negotiating down from someone else's number lets their number keep steering.

items.prompt: In the worked call, why did Dana's reframe to Marcus about the incumbent objection work as one short sentence, rather than a full feature tour?
choices: Marcus had already supplied the problem and its cost himself via the isolate question — the reframe only needed to connect a capability to that already-confirmed cost
Because Dana had, by that point in the call, run out of time left to spend on the call
Because Marcus had explicitly asked Dana at the outset to keep the pitch brief
Because a short reframe, per this unit, always performs better regardless of the context
items.explanation: Acknowledge and isolate had already done the hard work of surfacing the real, costly gap in Marcus's own words — the reframe just needed to point at the matching capability, not re-persuade from scratch.
items.reference:
🎯 short reframe = point at what's already confirmed, not persuade from scratch

Why: A long pitch is often a sign nobody yet knows what the prospect actually needs — Dana already knew, from Marcus's own answer.

items.prompt: What made a long, thorough pitch unnecessary at the reframe stage of Dana's call with Marcus?
choices: Acknowledge and isolate had already surfaced the real problem and its cost in Marcus's own words, so reframe just needed to match a capability to it
Marcus had, per the transcript, already decided to buy before the call even started
The product, as described in the call, only had one single feature worth mentioning at all
Long, thorough pitches are, per this unit, never appropriate in any sales conversation
items.explanation: The earlier steps had already done the work of finding the real concern — reframe's job at that point is narrow and specific, not a full persuasion effort from a standing start.
items.reference:
🎯 short reframe = point at what's already confirmed, not persuade from scratch

Why: A long pitch is often a sign nobody yet knows what the prospect actually needs — Dana already knew, from Marcus's own answer.

items.prompt: When Marcus said "$24,000 is too expensive," why did Dana restate the roughly $33,600/year cost of the overtime problem instead of immediately offering a lower number?
choices: To reset the anchor around the value Marcus had already confirmed, rather than negotiating down from list price with no reasoning attached
Because Dana had not, at that point in the call, yet calculated a discount worth offering
To stall the conversation until Marcus was the one to bring up a number first
Because restating the cost is, per this unit, legally required before any price can be discussed
items.explanation: Restating the confirmed cost re-anchors the conversation around value Marcus already agreed was real, instead of letting the conversation drift toward whichever number gets said first.
items.reference:
🎯 anchor reset: restate confirmed value ($33,600/yr cost), not just repeat list price

Why: A number backed by reasoning the prospect already agreed to moves a real budget line further than a bare repeated price or an immediate discount.

items.prompt: What would Dana have signaled by immediately offering a discount the moment Marcus said "too expensive," without restating the confirmed cost first?
choices: That the list price was never firm to begin with, weakening the anchor and inviting further pushback
That the product was, in that moment, more valuable than Marcus had originally realized
That the deal was, at that point, already lost regardless of what price got quoted
Nothing in particular — an immediate discount, per this unit, carries no signal either way
items.explanation: An instant discount, with no reasoning attached, signals the original price was never real — the same mistake Theo makes later in this level, and it invites the prospect to keep pushing for more.
items.reference:
🎯 anchor reset: restate confirmed value ($33,600/yr cost), not just repeat list price

Why: A number backed by reasoning the prospect already agreed to moves a real budget line further than a bare repeated price or an immediate discount.

items.prompt: What's the actual difference between "repeating the list price" and the "counter-anchoring" move Dana made?
choices: Counter-anchoring ties the number to a value the prospect already confirmed, rather than just repeating a number with no new reasoning behind it
Counter-anchoring, per this unit, always involves stating a higher number than the original list price
There is no real difference — both are, per this unit, the same negotiation move under different names
Counter-anchoring, per this unit, means refusing to discuss price again for the rest of the call
items.explanation: Simply repeating "$24,000" adds no new information; connecting that number to the $33,600/year cost Marcus already confirmed gives the prospect a reason the number holds, which is what actually resets the anchor.
items.reference:
🎯 anchor reset: restate confirmed value ($33,600/yr cost), not just repeat list price

Why: A number backed by reasoning the prospect already agreed to moves a real budget line further than a bare repeated price or an immediate discount.

items.prompt: What did Dana give up, and what did Dana get back, in the final trade with Marcus?
choices: Gave up $4,200/year off list price; got back a two-year locked term and a future reference call
Gave up the two-year term in exchange for a higher price than the original list price
Gave up nothing at all; Marcus simply agreed to pay the list price exactly as quoted
Gave up the reference call in exchange for a smaller initial contract than list price
items.explanation: Dana's final offer was $19,800/year (down from $24,000 list) locked for two years, in exchange for the two-year commitment itself plus a future reference call — value moving in both directions.
items.reference:
⚖️ gave: $4,200/yr off list — got: 2-yr locked term + future reference call

Why: Both sides gave something up and got something back — that's what keeps it a trade instead of a giveaway.

items.prompt: Why was the two-year locked term valuable to Dana beyond simply closing this one deal?
choices: It reduces the risk of losing the account after one year and locks the rate against a future price increase — real value, not just goodwill
It lets Dana avoid ever having to have a renewal conversation with Marcus again
It guarantees, per the call, that Marcus will refer at least two new prospects to Dana
It has, per this unit, no additional value beyond what a plain one-year term would offer
items.explanation: A two-year term reduces churn risk and protects against a future list-price increase eating into the deal's value — both concrete benefits to Dana, not just a nicer-sounding contract length.
items.reference:
⚖️ gave: $4,200/yr off list — got: 2-yr locked term + future reference call

Why: Both sides gave something up and got something back — that's what keeps it a trade instead of a giveaway.

items.prompt: If Dana had agreed to $19,800 with no term extension and no reference commitment from Marcus, what would that have been instead of a concession trade?
choices: A one-way discount — no exchange happened in return for the value given up
A stronger negotiation outcome than the one Dana actually reached with the two-year term
Still a valid trade, per this unit, since Marcus would have been satisfied with it either way
An anchoring move, per this unit, rather than a one-way discount with nothing given back

items.reference:
⚖️ gave: $4,200/yr off list — got: 2-yr locked term + future reference call

Why: Both sides gave something up and got something back — that's what keeps it a trade instead of a giveaway.

items.prompt: Theo's final price ($18,000 flat, no strings attached) was close to Dana's ($19,800 with terms). Why did the two calls still produce very different outcomes?
choices: Theo never confirmed whether $18,000 was a real ceiling, gave up the full amount with nothing received in return, and never secured the two-year term or reference
Theo's product demo was, in the transcript, technically worse than the one Dana gave
Theo quoted a higher list price at the outset of the call than Dana had quoted
The two calls, per the transcripts, actually produced identical outcomes in every respect

items.reference:
❌ Theo — argue, then cave for nothing back
✅ Dana — acknowledge/isolate, then trade

Why: Similar final numbers can hide very different deals — one gave margin away for nothing, the other traded it for real, ongoing value.

items.prompt: Why did Theo's response to "we already have something that works" damage the rest of the call, before pricing was even discussed?
choices: Listing feature advantages argued against a decision Marcus had already made, prompting Marcus to defend it and nearly end the call instead of disclosing the real overtime problem
Theo's stated features were, per the transcript, factually incorrect in several places
Theo spoke, per the transcript, too quietly during the demo portion of the call
Theo asked, per the transcript, too many isolating questions back to back
items.explanation: Arguing point-by-point against the spreadsheet put Marcus in the position of defending his own decision, which is exactly the dynamic that keeps a real, costly gap from surfacing.
items.reference:
❌ Theo — argue, then cave for nothing back
✅ Dana — acknowledge/isolate, then trade

items.prompt: If Marcus's isolate answer to the incumbent objection had instead been "it's fine, I just need to check with my director," what should change about the reframe that follows?
